=== Project No. 58481 _ Schaper Energy Consulting _ Supplemental Comments.pdf ===
                                      PUC PROJECT NO. 58481

                                                     §
    RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                          §        PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
   LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                        §
   STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                     §                     OF TEXAS
                                                     §
                                                     §


     SCHAPER ENERGY CONSULTING LLC SUPPLEMENTAL RESPONSE TO STAFF’s

                JANUARY 2, 2025 QUESTIONS RELATED TO DRAFT 16 TAC §25.194


                                          I.​ INTRODUCTION


           Schaper Energy Consulting LLC (“Respondent”) advises large load customers in ERCOT on

interconnection, utility coordination, and energy procurement. Respondent supports power development

for data center campuses, working directly with utilities and guiding clients through ERCOT’s large load

interconnection processes. Respondent’s clients represent a meaningful share of large load

interconnection activity in ERCOT, providing a clear view of process challenges and practical avenues

for improvement.


           Respondent respectfully submits the following comments in response to Commission Staff's

memorandum dated January 2, 2025, soliciting stakeholder input on the second draft of proposed 16 TAC

§25.194 relating to Large Load Interconnection Standards, the January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop,

and related stakeholder comments. Respondent appreciates the opportunity to participate in this

proceeding and commends Staff for its continued engagement with stakeholders on these important

matters.


           These comments are organized as follows: Section II includes Defined Terms, Section III

provides general observations regarding certain concepts introduced in the second draft and the

Workshop, and Section IV addresses Staff's Questions 1 through 16 in sequential order.


                                                                                                      1
                                         II.​ DEFINED TERMS


       For this response, “Utility” refers to Transmission Service Providers (“TSPs”), Municipally

Owned Utilities (“MOUs”), and Electric Cooperatives (“ECs”) that administer large load interconnections

and interface with the Interconnecting Large Load Entity (“ILLE”). Capitalized Planning Guide terms

(e.g., Large Load Interconnection Study (“LLIS”), Load Commissioning Plan (“LCP”), Independent

System Operator (“ISO”), etc.) are used as defined in the ERCOT Planning Guide.




                                                                                                     2
                                      III.​ GENERAL COMMENTS


Coordination with ERCOT's Batch Study Initiative


​       Several commenters have noted the relationship between this rulemaking and ERCOT's pending

batch study initiative, announced by ERCOT leadership at the Commission's December 18, 2025, open

meeting. While we acknowledge the need to improve ERCOT's planning study review process and have

been active in proposing solutions, we respectfully urge the Commission not to delay this rulemaking to

await alignment with an initiative for which ERCOT has not yet provided detailed public guidance.


        The objectives of this rulemaking carry significant market importance. Establishing appropriate

measures to ensure uniform financial commitment and providing market participants with greater clarity

on large load interconnection requirements will benefit all stakeholders and support continued economic

development in the State of Texas. These considerations warrant prompt action.


        Should the Commission determine that coordination with ERCOT's initiative is needed, we

recommend that Staff encourage ERCOT to accelerate advancement of its process to match the pace of

this rulemaking and that ERCOT play an active role in this proceeding to enhance coherence between the

resulting frameworks. Full alignment with an undefined process may not be achievable, and continued

progress on this rulemaking need not await that outcome.


        Additionally, the Commission should consider providing a transition period for projects at an

advanced stage of study, allowing these load customers sufficient time to substantiate their loads under the

current process. Considerable investment has been made in reliance on both the interim interconnection

processes and PGRR115, and these investments would be placed at risk by an abrupt transition to a new

framework.




                                                                                                          3
 Comments on Security Mechanism Structure and Staging


          We recommend that Staff adopt a staged approach to security requirements in which the amount,

refundability, and form of security escalate as interconnection studies are completed and deliverability

becomes more definitive. This approach aligns security obligations with the customer's capacity visibility

at each stage of the process, is consistent with comments from other stakeholders1, and is not precluded

by any language in Senate Bill 6 (“SB6”).


          Comments at the January 9, 2026, workshop revealed considerable uncertainty among market

participants regarding the proposed security mechanisms, specifically their form, timing, and

refundability, and how each attribute relates to security sizing. Central to this confusion is whether the

uniform financial commitment established by SB6 is intended as a proxy for interconnection costs or as a

financial demonstration of project seriousness. We believe the latter interpretation better reflects the

statute’s intent. Interconnection CIAC and security related to transmission system projects are more

appropriately reserved for later stages of the process, when costs can be estimated with reasonable

accuracy. The uniform financial commitment serves a distinct purpose: establishing queue discipline at

the outset, precisely when project-specific costs remain difficult to ascertain.


          The $100,000 per MW amount proposed in the January 2, 2026 draft, if required prior to study

completion, presents significant practical challenges for project financing regardless of refundability. At

typical developer costs of capital, the carrying costs over the implied holding period create substantial

losses, as other respondents have noted2. Security at this level effectively limits participation to entities

with access to parent guarantees or near-zero financing costs, excluding not only a significant portion of

the data center development market but also more traditional industrial load customers.




1
    Google/Lancium joint comments on Project 58481 dated December 18, 2025.
2
    Black Mountain comments to Project 58481 dated December 19, 2025.

                                                                                                           4
         To the extent security is required before definitive study results are available, we encourage Staff

to adopt a refundable requirement at a lower magnitude that legitimate customers can reasonably provide.

Based on median and average responses from twenty-two prior commenters3, an amount in the range of

$20,000 to $28,000 per MW would appropriately balance queue discipline with accessibility.


        We support linking initial security to gross load sizing, which encourages customers to calibrate

requested capacity to their development confidence and contractual offtake visibility. We further support

proposals to correlate per-MW security amounts with the timing of requested load ramps4. Near-term

energization requests present greater accommodation challenges for utilities and ERCOT and place more

strain on system-wide resource adequacy. Linking security to ramp pace introduces appropriate incentives

and decision points that reflect these realities


Credit of Costs Against Intermediate Agreement Security


        We respectfully suggest that costs incurred by customers under preliminary study, service, or

equipment agreements with the utility should offset the security amount required at the intermediate

agreement stage, rather than supplement it. Several other commenters have noted the same concern5.


        This approach would avoid duplicative layers of security and promote a streamlined framework in

which a single security agreement can be implemented, amended as circumstances evolve, and reconciled

against actual costs and executed interconnection agreements.


Preliminary Screening Study and Associated Security Implications


        We appreciate Staff's introduction of the preliminary screening study concept into this

rulemaking. We understand the intent may be to provide customers with an additional off-ramp earlier in

the interconnection process.

3
  Multiple Respondent Comments to Project 58481 dated December 1, 2025 through December 19, 2025.
4
  Cholla, Inc. comments to Project 58481, dated December 17, 2025.
5
  TIEC and Data Center Coalition comments during Jannaury 10, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                          5
         However, our experience with preliminary screening studies suggests they may provide limited

value for establishing project viability or supporting financing, particularly if conducted by an entity other

than the one ultimately determining firm capacity allocation. Such screening would likely be less

comprehensive than either a utility's serial Large Load Interconnection Study or ERCOT's forthcoming

batch process. Given data limitations, including the status of other substantiated loads under Planning

Guide Section 9.3.4.1 and facilities interconnection costs, a preliminary screening study may not reliably

indicate available capacity, timing, or cost. We also note that large load customers seeking preliminary

guidance could pursue independent screening through third-party engineering firms without consuming

utility resources, as is common practice today.


        Given these limitations, we recommend that the screening study not serve as a trigger for either

security non-refundability or an escalation in security magnitude unless the customer can be assured that

it accurately reflects available capacity. A preliminary batch study conducted by ERCOT may be the only

approach capable of achieving this objective, though its value may be limited if the batch is oversized or

includes unsubstantiated loads. We suggest Staff work closely with ERCOT to evaluate the predictive

value of any such screening study before relying upon it to trigger greater customer commitment.


        Accordingly, we recommend that amounts at risk under a preliminary security agreement be

limited to the proposed study fees until definitive capacity and cost information becomes available. We

support the framework introduced by other commenters6, whereby refundable security posted in advance

of studies transitions to at-risk status on a reasonable timeline following confirmation of capacity, creating

fair decision points throughout the process.




6
 Joint Comments of Google and Lancium to Project 58481, dated December 18, 2025 and January 10, 2026 Large
Load workshop comments and Rose City Partners January 10, 2026 Large Load workshop comments.

                                                                                                            6
                   IV.​ RESPONSE TO STAFF QUESTIONS DATED JANUARY 2, 2025


Question 1. Should the rule define “dynamic modeling” for large loads? If so, what definition should

be used?


           We support the requirement that an ILLE provide dynamic modeling information to the

interconnecting utility or, if the process transitions to an ERCOT-led batch study, to ERCOT. We note that

ERCOT is currently developing new standards based on its “Large Electronic Load (LEL) Modeling

Approach and DWG Survey Document Update” presentation dated December 18, 20257. Given this

ongoing work, requirements for dynamic modeling in large load interconnection studies remain in flux.

Accordingly, we respectfully suggest the Commission avoid overly prescriptive language in this area,

allowing flexibility to align with ERCOT's forthcoming standards as they are finalized.


Question 2. If the commission includes an “initial screening study” as an option that a large load

customer may request from an interconnecting utility prior to the initiation of a large load

interconnection study, how should the commission define “initial screening study”?


           We conditionally support the concept of an initial screening study and offer the following

observations for Staff's consideration. We refer Staff to our General Comments and the comments from

the Large Load Workshop8 for additional discussion of this topic.


           First, interconnecting utilities would likely conduct these studies using a more limited analytical

scope than a full Large Load Interconnection Study. Without a comprehensive analysis, an ILLE may not

have adequate visibility into the interconnecting utility's ability to serve the requested load. Staff may

wish to consider whether this limited scope could lead ILLEs to place undue reliance on preliminary

results.

7
  Electric Reliability Council of Texas (ERCOT), Dynamic Studies Team, Large Electronic Load (LEL) Modeling
Approach        and     DWG       Survey    Document    Update     (Dec.    18,     2025),    available  at
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025/12/19/LEL-Modeling-Approach-and-Survey-Update_Dec-18-2025_R03.pdf.
8
  Comments from Oncor, TIEC and LCRA in January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                            7
         Second, ERCOT's proposed batch study process may materially alter the inputs to any

transmission analysis and, consequently, affect capacity availability and interconnection timelines. An

initial screening study performed by an interconnecting utility prior to the batch study would not reflect

these changes and could therefore produce misleading results.


        In light of these considerations, we believe Staff should include this concept only if, in

coordination with interconnecting utilities or ERCOT, it can be determined that such screening studies

will provide meaningful value for this rulemaking. Otherwise, we respectfully suggest that these studies

remain voluntary and be conducted independently by the ILLE.


(a)​    What specific and preliminary information would an initial screening study need to identify for

        a large load customer to determine whether a site is feasible?


                If implemented, an initial screening study should, at a minimum, identify:


            a.​ whether existing substation and transmission facilities can accommodate all or a portion

                of the requested load without significant upgrades, including a realistic assessment of

                firm transmission headroom available to serve the load prior to any required system

                upgrades;

            b.​ a preliminary estimate of the timeline to energization based on current queue position and

                system constraints;

            c.​ whether the proposed interconnection point is viable from a transmission planning

                perspective; and

            d.​ any obvious fatal flaws that would render the site infeasible.


                To be useful to ILLEs, the study must provide actionable information, particularly

        regarding available capacity and realistic timelines, sufficient to support site selection and

        preliminary development decisions.


                                                                                                        8
 (b)​      What specific and preliminary information would the interconnecting utility need from the

          large load customer to perform an initial screening study?


                   The interconnecting utility should require, at a minimum:


                       a.​ the proposed point of interconnection, including GPS coordinates and requested

                           voltage level; and

                       b.​ the requested preliminary load ramp schedule, specified by month and year.


                   Depending on the scope of the screening analysis, the ILLE may also need to provide

          load characteristics in a format suitable for transmission planning personnel to evaluate

          steady-state system impacts.


(c)​      Should a fee be imposed on a large load customer for the interconnecting utility to conduct an

          initial screening study? If so, what amount should be used for a standardized initial screening

          study fee?


                   A fee of $10,000 to $20,000 would be reasonable for an initial screening study and in line

          with the view of other commenters9, reflecting the limited engineering effort required, provided

          those items outlined in item (a) above can be reliably included. This fee should be credited toward

          the full LLIS study fee and deducted from the previously contemplated Study Fees in the current

          draft, regardless of whether the ILLE elects to proceed or withdraw.


(d)​      What is an appropriate time frame for an interconnecting utility to complete an initial

          screening study?


                   The 30-day timeframe is appropriate for an initial screening study conducted by the

          interconnecting utility, as such studies require only desktop analysis rather than detailed


9
    Centerpoint Energy and Monarch Energy comments at January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                           9
         modeling. However, Staff should clarify whether the interconnecting utility or ERCOT will

        perform these studies and consider whether the additional workload may exacerbate existing

        resource constraints affecting study timelines across the interconnection queue.


(e)​    How would this initial screening study differ from today's current processes?


                Today's processes effectively require the interconnecting TSP to perform a full Large

        Load Interconnection Study before providing meaningful feasibility information, essentially

        treating comprehensive studies as an initial screening. A standardized initial screening study, if

        properly implemented, can identify infeasible project sites earlier in the process and reduce

        unnecessary demands on utility or ERCOT engineering resources, subject to the limitations

        identified above.


Question 3. Should the commission maintain the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set

forth in Attachment C? If not, what definition should be used?


        Regardless of the definition Staff ultimately adopts, this rulemaking should address which entity

is responsible for conducting the LLIS when a transmission-only utility and the TSP serving the

certificated retail provider are different entities. The current rules do not clearly establish whether a

transmission-only utility may perform the LLIS in such circumstances, and we have encountered

inconsistent approaches across projects as a result.


        We recommend that the Commission designate a single entity responsible for both the LLIS and

all consolidated documentation for the ILLE. This role should belong to either the unified TDSP or a

single designated transmission and distribution or generation and transmission cooperative holding

contractual service rights within the certificated retail service territory of a retail cooperative. The rules

should also clarify how an ILLE should coordinate with the various entities that may be involved in a

transmission-level interconnection, including transmission-only utilities, transmission and distribution


                                                                                                           10
 cooperatives, TSPs serving municipally owned utilities, and electric cooperatives acting solely as

distribution service providers.


        Finally, we request that the Commission consider grandfathering provisions for projects where an

ILLE has already initiated the LLIS process with a transmission-only utility. Permitting completion of

those studies would prevent disruption and protect investments made in reasonable reliance on the prior

regulatory framework.


Question 4. If the commission maintains the definition for an interconnecting utility that is set forth in

Attachment C, what framework should the rule establish for ensuring that the interconnecting

transmission service provider receives the required security and CIAC in instances where the

certificated retail utility and interconnecting transmission service provider are different entities?


        We refer Staff to our response to Question 3 on this matter.


Question 5. For a large load customer that seeks to expand capacity at an existing site, should the total

capacity or only the new incremental capacity at that site be subject to the rule requirements? Why?


        We respectfully decline to respond to this question at this time and refer Staff to the comments

from the January 9, 2026, workshop.


Question 6. Currently, ERCOT Planning Guide §9.2.1(1)(b) requires a large load customer to follow

the criteria subject to the large load interconnection study process if the large load customer modifies

an existing load facility that increases the aggregate peak demand of the facility by 75 MW or more.

Should the commission maintain this threshold for purposes of the rule? Or should any modification

that increases the aggregate peak demand of the facility to 75 MW or more be required to satisfy the

criteria in the rule?




                                                                                                        11
            We respectfully decline to respond to this question at this time and refer Staff to the comments

from the January 9, 2026 workshop.


Question 7. Does an interconnecting utility, at the intermediate agreement phase, have sufficient

information to be able to estimate the costs of significant equipment and services and to estimate

contribution in aid of construction?


           As other commenters have noted10, we do not believe the interconnecting utility will have

sufficient information at the intermediate agreement stage, as currently drafted, to estimate CIAC with

precision. While preliminary cost ranges may be available for substation equipment and direct-assigned

facilities, system upgrade costs depend on study outcomes that are not yet available at that point in the

transmission planning process. Accordingly, if the proposed definition of CIAC includes system upgrades,

reliable cost estimates may not be feasible until later stages of the interconnection process.


(a)​       If so, should the rule require payment of the $100,000 per megawatt security at the time the

           request for interconnection is submitted? And require estimated security for significant

           equipment and services and contribution in aid of construction at the intermediate agreement

           stage, subject to a true up based on actual costs identified at the interconnection agreement

           stage?


                    We would refer Staff to our General Comments on this matter.


Question 8. Should the commission expand the criteria for demonstrating site control to include either

site control over an electrical substation combined with exclusive development rights at a designated

interconnection point or an exclusivity agreement with an existing generation resource for a proposed

net metering arrangement?




10
     Centerpoint Energy, STEC, Cholla, and AEP Texas comments at the January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                            12
         We believe the existing site control language is sufficient as drafted. Requiring the ILLE to

demonstrate site control over an existing electrical substation is impractical, as these facilities are

typically utility-owned or leased by utilities from third parties with whom the ILLE has no contractual

relationship. Moreover, such a requirement is unnecessary where the interconnecting utility or the ILLE

has obtained voluntary easements or holds CCN authority for the transmission infrastructure required to

reach the ILLE's facility. The existing site control standards, which focus on the ILLE's load facility

location, appropriately allocate responsibility for transmission infrastructure to the interconnecting utility.


Question 9. What value may be gained from collecting data about project developers and end-use

customers for purposes of developing ERCOT’s load forecasts?


        We recommend that Staff rely primarily on demonstrations of site control and the proposed

security requirements, rather than disclosures regarding end-use customer relationships, as inputs for load

forecasting. Site control and financial security are objective, verifiable indicators of project commitment.

In contrast, end-use customer relationships may be subject to confidentiality restrictions that limit their

usefulness for load forecasting, transmission planning, or resource adequacy, or may change as projects

progress through development.


        As noted in our General Comments, the proposed security requirements already present

significant financial commitments that substantiate load projections. These measures, combined with site

control demonstrations, provide a sufficient basis for forecasting without relying on customer relationship

disclosures that may disadvantage developer-led projects.         Such projects play an important role in

bringing new load-serving infrastructure to market, and many secure end-use customers only after

advancing through early development stages. Staff should ensure that any use of classification data

collected as part of this demonstration does not create a framework that disadvantages projects based

solely on their development structure.




                                                                                                             13
 Question 10. How should an interconnecting utility treat interest accrued from cash security?


         Interest should accrue to the benefit of the ILLE. As other commenters have noted, it is

exceedingly rare for interconnecting utilities to hold cash for security purposes; therefore, Staff may have

limited need to address this matter11.


(a)​     What interest rate should apply?


         Rather than establishing a new methodology, we support the continued use of the interest rate

currently adopted and periodically updated by the Commission12. This approach provides regulatory

consistency and relies on an established benchmark that market participants can readily reference.


(b)​     What process should be used to return interest to the large load customer?


         If security is held in the form of cash for a period exceeding one year, accrued interest should be

distributed to the ILLE on a quarterly basis beginning after the first anniversary of the deposit, calculated

at the applicable rate specified in our response to Question 10(a). Upon final refund of any unused

security, remaining accrued interest should be returned to the ILLE, net of any amounts applied to

outstanding costs. The interest calculation should be provided to the ILLE upon request and included in

the final accounting statement.


Question 11. What is the average CIAC that is charged to a large load customer seeking to

interconnect today?


         We respectfully decline to propose a specific prescriptive value, as CIAC amounts can vary

significantly depending on interconnection topology, site-specific conditions, and utilization of existing



11
  CenterPoint Energy comments in January 10, 2026 Large Load Workshop.
12
   See 16 Tex. Admin. Code § 25.24(g) (establishing annual interest rate on customer deposits); Public Utility
Commission          of      Texas,        Historical       Interest     Rates       on       Customer          Deposits,
https://ftp.puc.texas.gov/public/puct-info/industry/electric/reports/HRates/HistRates.pdf (last visited Jan. 12, 2026).

                                                                                                                     14
 interconnection facilities as noted by other commenters13. Given this inherent variability, we believe it

may be challenging for Staff to use CIAC as a uniform measure of financial commitment across all

projects, and we encourage Staff to consider this limitation when evaluating potential threshold-based

approaches.


Question 12. For what period of time should a large load customer be expected to operate after

energization but before the interconnecting utility issues a final refund of any unused security,

collateral, or CIAC in order to balance the state’s interests in supporting business development and

minimizing the potential for stranded infrastructure costs?


           Our position on this question depends on whether the current draft language, which would

incorporate system upgrades into the customer CIAC, is retained in the final rule.


           If the current CIAC construct is maintained, we respectfully suggest that customer security be

released upon energization, as the customer will have satisfied all direct and system-impact cost

obligations by payment of a non-refundable CIAC, thereby eliminating further risk to ratepayers. Under

this framework, we are uncertain about which unused security obligations would remain and would

appreciate the Staff's clarification on this point.


           If Staff reverts to a customer-secured framework for system upgrades with traditional

postage-stamp cost recovery for system upgrades, we would support releasing security on an “earlier-of”

basis tied to either (1) the load achieving demand thresholds specified in its Load Commissioning Plan, or

(2) an outside date triggered by the load reaching approximately 80% of the gross capacity that was

studied for transmission upgrades. This approach would help ensure that customers utilize an appropriate

level of capacity and that infrastructure constructed to support their projects is not stranded.




13
     Satoshi Energy and TIEC comments in January 10, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                       15
            We note that, as a practical matter, utilities have observed that transmission improvements rarely

go unused because a load customer fails to materialize. Accordingly, the risk of stranded investment that

security is intended to mitigate may be more limited than initially anticipated14.


Question 13. If the commission adopts a process whereby ERCOT, not the interconnecting utility,

reallocates capacity on a system-wide basis through a batch study process, what parameters should the

commission establish for such a process?


           We respectfully refer Staff to our General Comments for a more detailed discussion of this matter.

While we appreciate the importance of regulatory coordination, we believe it may be challenging, in

practice, to fully align this rulemaking with a pending process for which details have not yet been made

publicly available. Accordingly, we would respectfully suggest that this rulemaking proceed on its current

timeline rather than be delayed in anticipation of that process, particularly given the uncertainty

surrounding the expected duration of that proceeding.


           Further, the Commission may need to establish transition provisions for projects currently in the

ERCOT queue to provide clear expectations for in-progress interconnections and avoid unnecessary

disruption. As noted by other commenters, projects with serial planning studies already under ERCOT

review warrant particular attention, as these ILLEs have made substantial investments in reliance on the

existing framework15. Clear communication to the market regarding the treatment of these projects will

help ensure that capital commitments are not placed at unnecessary risk during any potential transition

period.


Question 14. Is 60 days a sufficient time frame for an interconnecting utility to issue a required

refund?


           We believe this is an adequate timeframe for an interconnecting utility to issue a refund.
14
     Oncor comments to January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.
15
     Satoshi Energy comments to January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                          16
 Question 15. What changes should be made to Attachment C to account for the fact that municipally

owned utilities and electric cooperatives have exclusive jurisdiction over retail rates in their service

territory?


           We respectfully decline to respond to this question at this time.


Question 16. Is there anything else that the commission should consider in its implementation of

PURA §37.0561?


           We respectfully recommend that Staff consider the following additional matters in the

Commission's implementation of PURA §37.0561:


           First, the Commission should carefully consider the impact of ERCOT's proposed batch study

process on queue prioritization. Customers who entered the interconnection queue at an earlier date must

not be disadvantaged by later-filed applications, nor should their allocated capacity be diminished through

inclusion in a batch study, particularly where such customers have already funded and substantially

completed studies under PGRR115 or preceding interim processes16. Socializing the study costs or

capacity allocations of early-queue customers with those who submitted interconnection requests at a

materially later date would undermine the foundational principle of queue priority and create inequitable

outcomes for customers who acted in timely reliance on established procedures. Additionally, the

Commission should consider providing a grace period of at least 90 days for projects at an advanced stage

of study to transition to the new requirements for substantiating load under ERCOT Planning Guide

Sections 9.4 and 9.5. Such a provision would mitigate significant market disruption and provide

reasonable accommodation for customers who have made substantial investments in reliance on prior

procedures.




16
     Tract comments to January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                        17
         Second, we would support the Commission encouraging ERCOT to fast-track the adoption and

implementation of PGRR134 alongside ERCOT’s batch study process17. This planning guide revision

request allows large load customers to elect Controllable Load Resource (CLR) status during their

interconnection study, enabling TSPs to model them as dispatchable loads that can be curtailed to their

Low Power Consumption level. This may accelerate energization timelines by mitigating transmission

constraints through dispatch rather than requiring network upgrades.


        Third, we respectfully suggest that the Commission consider expanding ERCOT's regular

reporting requirements on interconnection queue status to include more transparent and granular

information on the progress of planning studies, as well as delineate projects approved with conditions

tied to transmission upgrades from those approved without such conditions, enabling market participants

and policymakers to better assess queue dynamics and infrastructure development timelines. Further, we

believe there is value in a private reporting dashboard (‘LIOO’) tracking ILLE project status that is

accessible to ERCOT, the interconnecting utility, and the ILLE, as suggested by other commenters18


        Fourth, we encourage Staff to consider the implications of ERCOT's expanding role in

establishing load operational requirements and the potential impact on market competitiveness. As noted

in our prior comments on proposed language in §25.194(l) and as reflected in the comments of other

market stakeholders19, permitting ERCOT to exercise broad operational authority over load behavior may

have serious operational consequences for certain load classes or result in conservative standards that

diminish Texas's competitiveness as a destination for large-scale load development. Recent nodal

operating guide revision requests, such as NOGRR282, illustrate this concern. We respectfully submit that

any expansion of ERCOT's operational authority should be considered alongside market-based solutions

that address ERCOT's technical concerns while preserving the state's competitive position.



17
   Cholla comments to January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.
18
   Google, TEBA, and Cholla comments at January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.
19
   TIEC comments at January 9, 2026 Large Load Workshop.

                                                                                                      18
                                                V.​ CLOSING


        We appreciate the opportunity to provide additional input on Project No. 58481 and to respond to

Staff’s questions regarding 16 TAC §25.194. We value Staff’s careful work in developing the draft

language and welcome continued engagement as the rulemaking progresses. We respectfully submit that

these recommendations will support business growth while maintaining cost responsibility, transparency,

and reliability, and ensuring sufficient financial commitment to prevent stranded infrastructure.




                                                            Respectfully submitted,

                                                            Schaper Energy Consulting, LLC
                                                            3006 Brazos St., Ste. 200

                                   PUC PROJECT NO. 58481


 RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                        §         PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §                     OF TEXAS
STANDARDS UNDER PURA §37.0561                   §

   SCHAPER ENERGY CONSULTING LLC COMMENTS EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

●​ Batch Study Coordination: Do not delay this rulemaking for ERCOT's undefined batch study
   process; ERCOT should accelerate to match this rulemaking's pace.
●​ Security Staging: Adopt staged security that escalates as studies progress; uniform financial
   commitment is for queue discipline, not cost recovery.
●​ Security Amount: $100K/MW pre-study is prohibitive; $20K–$28K/MW is appropriate based
   on the commenter median/average.
●​ Cost Credit: Prior study/equipment costs paid to utilities should offset intermediate agreement
   security.
●​ Screening Study Caution: Screening studies have limited value without comprehensive data;
   they should not trigger non-refundability or security escalation.
●​ Q1 (Dynamic Modeling): Support requirement but avoid prescriptive definitions; defer to
   ERCOT's evolving LEL modeling standards.
●​ Q2 (Initial Screening Study): Conditionally support; limited analytical scope may mislead
   ILLEs; $10K–$20K fee is reasonable; 30 days appropriate; should credit toward LLIS fee.
●​ Q3 (Interconnecting Utility Definition): Clarify which entity conducts LLIS when a
   transmission-only utility differs from a retail TSP; designate a single responsible entity;
   grandfather in-flight projects.
●​ Q7 (CIAC Estimate at Intermediate Stage): Utilities lack sufficient information to estimate
   CIAC if it includes system upgrades; reliable estimates require completion of later-stage studies.
●​ Q8 (Site Control Criteria): Existing language sufficient; requiring substation control is
   impractical and unnecessary.
●​ Q9 (Developer/End-User Data): Rely on site control and security, not end-user disclosures;

                                      III. GENERAL COMMENTS


Coordination with ERCOT's Batch Study Initiative


        Several commenters have noted the relationship between this rulemaking and ERCOT's pending

batch study initiative, announced by ERCOT leadership at the Commission's December 18, 2025, open

meeting. While we acknowledge the need to improve ERCOT's planning study review process and have

been active in proposing solutions, we respectfully urge the Commission not to delay this rulemaking to

await alignment with an initiative for which ERCOT has not yet provided detailed public guidance.


        The objectives of this rulemaking carry significant market importance. Establishing appropriate

measures to ensure uniform financial commitment and providing market participants with greater clarity

on large load interconnection requirements will benefit all stakeholders and support continued economic

development in the State of Texas. These considerations warrant prompt action.


        Should the Commission determine that coordination with ERCOT's initiative is needed, we

recommend that Staff encourage ERCOT to accelerate advancement of its process to match the pace of

this rulemaking and that ERCOT play an active role in this proceeding to enhance coherence between the

resulting frameworks. Full alignment with an undefined process may not be achievable, and continued

progress on this rulemaking need not await that outcome.


        Additionally, the Commission should consider providing a transition period for projects at an

advanced stage of study, allowing these load customers sufficient time to substantiate their loads under the

current process. Considerable investment has been made in reliance on both the interim interconnection

processes and PGRR115, and these investments would be placed at risk by an abrupt transition to a new

framework.

 Comments on Security Mechanism Structure and Staging


        We recommend that Staff adopt a staged approach to security requirements in which the amount,

refundability, and form of security escalate as interconnection studies are completed and deliverability

becomes more definitive. This approach aligns security obligations with the customer's capacity visibility

at each stage of the process, is consistent with comments from other stakeholdersl, and is not precluded

by any language in Senate Bill 6 ("SB6")


        Comments at the January 9,2026, workshop revealed considerable uncertainty among market

participants regarding the proposed security mechanisms, specifically their form, timing, and

refundability, and how each attribute relates to security sizing. Central to this confusion is whether the

uniform financial commitment established by SB6 is intended as a proxy for interconnection costs or as a

financial demonstration of project seriousness. We believe the latter interpretation better reflects the

statute's intent. Interconnection CMC and security related to transmission system projects are more

appropriately reserved for later stages of the process, when costs can be estimated with reasonable

accuracy. The uniform financial commitment serves a distinct purpose: establishing queue discipline at

the outset, precisely when project-specific costs remain difficult to ascertain.


        The $100,000 per MW amount proposed in the January 2,2026 draft, if required prior to study

completion, presents significant practical challenges for project financing regardless of refundability. At

typical developer costs of capital, the carrying costs over the implied holding period create substantial

losses, as other respondents have noted2 Security at this level effectively limits participation to entities

with access to parent guarantees or near-zero financing costs, excluding not only a significant portion of

the data center development market but also more traditional industrial load customers.

         However, our experience with preliminary screening studies suggests they may provide limited

value for establishing project viability or supporting financing, particularly if conducted by an entity other

than the one ultimately determining firm capacity allocation. Such screening would likely be less

comprehensive than either a utility's serial Large Load Interconnection Study or ERCOT's forthcoming

batch process. Given data limitations, including the status of other substantiated loads under Planning

Guide Section 9.3.4.1 and facilities interconnection costs, a preliminary screening study may not reliably

indicate available capacity, timing, or cost. We also note that large load customers seeking preliminary

guidance could pursue independent screening through third-party engineering firms without consuming

utility resources, as is common practice today.


        Given these limitations, we recommend that the screening study not serve as a trigger for either

security non-refundability or an escalation in security magnitude unless the customer can be assured that

it accurately reflects available capacity. A preliminary batch study conducted by ERCOT may be the only

approach capable of achieving this objective, though its value may be limited ifthe batch is oversized or

includes unsubstantiated loads. We suggest Staff work closely with ERCOT to evaluate the predictive

value of any such screening study before relying upon it to trigger greater customer commitment.


        Accordingly, we recommend that amounts at risk under a preliminary security agreement be

limited to the proposed study fees until definitive capacity and cost information becomes available. We

support the framework introduced by other commenterst whereby refundable security posted in advance

of studies transitions to at-risk status on a reasonable timeline following confirmation of capacity, creating

fair decision points throughout the process.

    ILLEs; $10K-$20K fee is reasonable; 30 days appropriate; should credit toward LLIS fee.
•   Q3 (Interconnecting Utility Definition): Clarify which entity conducts LLIS when a
    transmission-only utility differs from a retail TSP; designate a single responsible entity;
    grandfather in-flight projects.
•   Q7 (CIAC Estimate at Intermediate Stage): Utilities lack sufficient information to estimate
    CMC if it includes system upgrades; reliable estimates require completion of later-stage studies.
•   Q8 (Site Control Criteria): Existing language sufficient; requiring substation control is
    impractical and unnecessary.
•   Q9 (Developer/End-User Data): Rely on site control and security, not end-user disclosures;
    avoid disadvantaging developer-led projects that secure customers later in development.
•   Q10 (Interest on Cash Security): Interest accrues to ILLE; use existing PUC deposit rate;
    quarterly distribution after one year; include in final accounting.
•   Qll (Average CIAC): Declined to propose a specific value; CIAC varies too widely to serve as a
    uniform commitment measure.
•   Q12 (Security Release Timing): If CIAC includes system upgrades - release at energization. If
    traditional postage-stamp recovery - release upon earlier of (1) LCP demand thresholds or (2)
    -80% of studied capacity.
•   Q13 (Batch Study Parameters): Do not delay rulemaking for undefined ERCOT process;
    establish transition provisions for projects already in queue with serial studies under PGRR115.
•   Q14 (60-Day Refund Period): Adequate.
